article.title: TrumpCare
article.author: Paul deLespinasse
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Now that Democrats will control both house of Congress, one naturally wonders whether they can work with President Trump. A hopeful sign has come from the new senator from Michigan. Abdul El-Sayed wants to enact Medicare For All. He recently suggested that it be called TrumpCare ! Since the president loves to have things named for himself, this is a brilliant idea. Getting Trump’s support would greatly improve insurance reform’s chances of getting through Congress. Most Republicans would have to fall in line. Don’t consider this idea impossible. After all, it was the militant anti-Communist Richard Nixon who ended America’s total hostility to Communist China. And President Trump himself has indicated possible interest in the idea, since he reposted El-Sayed’s mockup of a TrumpCare gold card on his social media site. Related: Impeachment Could Become A Powerful Tool, But Probably Not Against A President The idea of enlisting Trump to enact Medicare For All is not a new one. During his first administration the New York Times reported that his friend Christopher Ruddy—founder and CEO of conservative NewsMax—was urging him to support a single-payer insurance system to replace Obamacare. This did not amaze me. Single-payer would promote conservative values like efficiency and simplicity. And it would eliminate separate governmental insurance programs for veterans, children, native Americans, and the poor. Strong presidential leadership could help overcome the chief political obstacle to insurance reform—how it would be financed. Strong leadership is essential here. Reform supporters grossly underestimate how much income taxes must be increased. Medical care, now about one fifth of GDP, cannot be financed by a small tax increase. Opponents—including powerful vested medical and insurance interests—take advantage of a general misunderstanding of how much people are already paying for insurance. They claim the program would leave less money in people’s pockets, which is not true. Most American families get insurance through their jobs and are unaware that as workers they are paying for all of its very high cost. They only see what they pay directly , the “employees’ share” plus their own deductibles and co-pays. They don’t realize that they are also paying the so-called “employers share”, the major portion of their insurance costs, indirectly in the form of lower wages. Employers pay for workers’ insurance out of the same pot from which they pay wages and salaries. What they remit for insurance is not available for wages. Americans will be comparing an obvious tax increase with what looks like a much smaller expense in the present system. Related: One Sided View of Preposterous Lawsuit At PBS But the new system will actually be cheaper because the current system is horribly inefficient. It features many different insurance companies and insurance policies, each with its own coverage, exclusions, and “in-network” doctors and hospitals. Coping with this complexity costs the average doctor around $80,000-$100,000 per year for clerical assistance, costs that must be paid for by patients or their self-financed insurance. And the insurance companies have considerable administrative expenses, dividends, and high executive salaries. A single-payer system, eliminating billing complexity and private profits, would greatly reduce the total cost of medical care. The large tax increase needed to support insurance would therefore cost the average worker less than he or she is already paying, directly and indirectly. Employers, no longer remitting large amounts to insure their workers, should be required to pass those savings along as wage increases. This would both be fair and make selling the program to the public easier. Selling the program to the public is where Donald Trump—skilled at getting public attention and selling his ideas—could come in. It might take someone like him to convince people that single-payer insurance would leave them, on average, with a bit more cash in their pockets. In an era when AI may be destroying jobs, single-payer’s decoupling of insurance from employment would also relieve a great deal of anxiety. Democrats, despite reservations about Trump, should take advantage of his skills to advance their policy priorities if he is interested in co-operating. Related: A Major Political Question: To Whom Did God Give Land? One caveat though: Let’s not assume that the new program should just be an expansion of Medicare to everyone. The president should appoint a task force of experts to study the strengths and weaknesses of foreign medical insurance systems. The task force should report its findings and recommendations within one year, so that Congress could enact a program covering everyone before Mr. Trump’s term expires. Any activity comprising a fifth of the GDP cannot be turned on a dime. The transition from the current insurance system would need to be carefully planned to make it as graceful and easy on everybody as possible. Go for it, Senator-elect El-Sayed! Go for it, President Trump! Let’s hear it for TrumpCare!
